questions.q: What is a backup file created by a text editor with a tilde suffix?
o: An encrypted copy of the source code stored in /tmp
An automatic backup copy of a file saved as filename~ while the original is being edited
A compressed archive of the entire web application
A log file recording every change made during an editing session
questions.x: Editors like Vim and Emacs create filename~ as a backup while you edit filename. If these files are deployed to production, they can expose the original source code to anyone who requests them.
questions.h: Many editors append a single special character to the filename when saving a backup. Which character is it?

questions.q: Why are editor backup files a security risk on production web servers?
o: They execute automatically when the server starts
They may be served as plain text by the web server, leaking source code including class names, property names, and dangerous logic
They overwrite the live application files on every request
They contain hardcoded admin passwords by default
questions.x: Backup files often contain the full source of the original file. If the web server serves them without executing PHP or other server-side code, an attacker can read class definitions, magic methods, and other details needed to craft exploits.
questions.h: The risk is not that the backup runs. It is that the backup gets served as readable text instead of being blocked.

questions.q: In the PHP deserialization lab, how was the CustomTemplate class source code obtained?
o: Through an SQL injection in the login form
By requesting CustomTemplate.php~, the editor backup file hinted at in an HTML comment
By decompiling the PHP bytecode from the session cookie
Through a public GitHub repository linked in the page footer
questions.x: An HTML comment hinted at CustomTemplate.php. Requesting the file directly would execute it, but appending ~ returned the backup as plain text, revealing the class name, properties, and the dangerous __destruct() logic.
questions.h: The writeup found a hint in an HTML comment. What suffix did they append to the PHP filename to get source instead of execution?

questions.q: Why does requesting CustomTemplate.php directly not reveal the source code?
o: PHP files are always encrypted on the server
The web server executes PHP files and returns only the output, not the source
PHP files require authentication to access
The .php extension is blocked by all web servers
questions.x: When a web server processes a .php file, it runs the PHP interpreter and sends the result to the client. The source code never appears in the response. Backup files with a ~ suffix are typically not processed as PHP.
questions.h: Think about what happens when you visit a .php URL versus a .php~ URL on a typical Apache or nginx setup.

questions.q: What is the most direct deployment fix for editor backup file leaks?
o: Rename all PHP files to .html
Ensure backup files (~, .bak, .swp) are never deployed to production and configure the web server to block access to them
Disable PHP magic methods in production
Move all source code to client-side JavaScript
questions.x: Backup files should be excluded from deployment via .gitignore and blocked at the web server level. Even if accidentally committed, server rules denying access to *~ and *.bak patterns prevent source code exposure.
questions.h: Two layers help: keep backup files out of the deployment, and block them at the web server if they slip through anyway.
